analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to cover contraception and related care with no deductibles or copays.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 18, 2025 with three bipartisan cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee; no vote has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, Medicare generally does not treat contraception as a covered benefit, so some women on Medicare — largely women with disabilities under 65 — can face deductibles and coinsurance for birth control pills, IUD insertion, and related visits. This bill writes contraception into Medicare law: Part B would cover contraceptive services (counseling, exams, device insertion and removal) with no deductible or copay, and Part D drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans would have to cover contraceptive drugs at no cost-sharing, starting in 2027. It also requires HHS and congressional investigators to study remaining gaps, including which health plans still don't cover contraception for free.
analysis.who_benefits: Women on Medicare who could still become pregnant — mostly beneficiaries under 65 who qualify through disability — gain coverage of contraceptive drugs, counseling, exams, and device insertion and removal with no deductible or copay starting in 2027. Dual-eligible Medicare/Medicaid beneficiaries gain a guarantee that their contraceptive coverage is at least as good as their Medicaid coverage. Taxpayers and Medicare beneficiaries collectively bear the added cost.

how_it_helps.text: Adds contraceptive items and services — including counseling, exams, device insertion and removal, ultrasound, and side-effect management — to Medicare Part B coverage, with no deductible and no cost-sharing, starting in 2027.
Requires Medicare Part D prescription drug plans and Part C Medicare Advantage plans to cover contraceptive drugs with no deductible, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing.
Requires the HHS Secretary to make sure dual-eligible (Medicare plus Medicaid) beneficiaries get contraceptive coverage at least as comprehensive as their Medicaid coverage.

Orders HHS to study drug coverage for Medicare beneficiaries with disabilities and the Government Accountability Office to study which health plans — commercial, Medicaid, Medicare, and TRICARE — still fail to cover or charge for contraception.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government (and Medicare Advantage and Part D plans, who must absorb the no-cost-sharing requirement) pays for the new benefit, costs ultimately spread across taxpayers and premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds federal spending: Medicare would pay providers 100 percent of the charge for contraceptive services and plans would have to cover contraceptive drugs with no cost-sharing, costs ultimately borne by taxpayers and by Medicare Advantage and Part D plans and their enrollees.

The bill does not help the majority of Medicare beneficiaries who are past reproductive age, and it leaves commercial insurance, TRICARE, and over-the-counter contraceptive coverage to future studies rather than fixing them (Section 4), so the 'coverage gap' it closes is a narrow one.
Implementation depends on the HHS Secretary writing guidance for contraceptive counseling coverage, so the practical reach of the benefit would depend on how a future administration interprets it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: free contraception for the relatively small group of reproductive-age women on Medicare, most of whom have disabilities and currently face cost-sharing or coverage gaps. The cost is higher federal and plan spending on prescription drugs and services, spread across all taxpayers and beneficiaries. The bill is also honest about its limits — it commissions studies on the parts of the system (commercial plans, TRICARE, over-the-counter drugs) it does not fix, rather than claiming to close every coverage gap. On the whole it is a modest, well-designed expansion with few downsides beyond cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it now sits with no hearing, vote, or further action.

narrative.text: The Senate introduced the bill on December 18, 2025 and immediately referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action has been taken since the referral; the bill has not been scheduled for committee consideration or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won yet; nothing has happened beyond introduction, so Medicare beneficiaries still pay out of pocket for contraception.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — bill untouched in committee

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: Senate Committee on Finance
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action on it; whether it advances depends on this committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has bipartisan sponsorship at introduction — one Democrat and two Republicans — with three cosponsors total.

industries.industry: Insurers (Medicare Advantage and Part D plans)
industries.note: They gain a new federally required benefit to administer; plans are paid for covering contraceptive drugs but must do so with no member cost-sharing.

Their products become a mandatory no-cost-sharing Part D benefit, expanding the paying customer base. This entrenches prescription contraceptives as the covered channel while the bill only studies, rather than covers, over-the-counter options.
Medicare becomes a paying payer for contraceptive counseling, insertions, and follow-up care it previously often did not cover, at 100 percent of charges up to the payment basis.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with the Senate Finance Committee, which controls most health entitlement legislation. Late-session introductions of this kind rarely reach the floor on their own; without a committee markup or attachment to a larger Medicare package, it will likely sit without action unless one of its three sponsors pushes it into a broader health bill.
